column4: ### Genesis: The God Who Dwells With His Creation
column5: ### Genesis: God Who Dwells with His Creation

column4: A central theme in the narrative of God is His **desire to dwell** with His creation. This is clear in the stories throughout Genesis. Across its fifty chapters and genealogies from Adam (the first man) through Joseph (that last major figure in the book of Genesis, the last significant leader of God’s people before Moses), there is a period of approximately ~2,400 years. We can see through these stories the consistency of God’s goodness despite man’s wickedness.
column5: A central theme in God's story is His desire to dwell with His creation—the desire to dwell together. This is evident throughout the narrative of Genesis. Across its fifty chapters, the genealogy from Adam (the first man) to Joseph (the last major figure in Genesis, the last significant leader of God's people before Moses) spans approximately ~2,400 years. Through these stories we find God's unchanging goodness despite human wickedness.

column4: In Genesis, God establishes relationship with select individuals.
column5: In Genesis, God enters into relationship with chosen individuals.

column4: 1.  **Adam and Eve** - The first humans, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden. God walks and talks with them, giving them instructions and establishing a relationship of mutual love and obedience. However, this relationship is impacted by their disobedience in eating from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil (Genesis 1-3).
column5: 1.  **Adam and Eve** - The first humans, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden. God walked with them, spoke to them, gave them instructions, and established a relationship of mutual love and obedience. However, this relationship was affected by their disobedience when they ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Genesis 1-3).

column4: 2.  **Cain** - Although Cain ultimately rebels by murdering his brother Abel, God speaks directly to him, warning him about the danger of sin and offering him guidance before the murder. Even after Cain’s punishment, God marks him to protect him from harm (Genesis 4).
column5: 2.  **Cain** - Though Cain ultimately rebels by killing his brother Abel, God speaks to him directly, warning him of the danger of sin and giving guidance before the murder. Even after Cain’s punishment, God put a mark on him and protected him from harm (Genesis 4).

column4: 3.  **Noah** - God establishes a unique relationship with Noah, a righteous man, in a time of widespread corruption. God commands Noah to build an ark to save his family and the animals from the Flood. Afterward, God makes a covenant with Noah, promising never again to destroy the earth with a flood and establishing the rainbow as a sign of this covenant (Genesis 6-9).
column5: 3.  **Noah** - In a time when corruption was widespread, God formed a unique relationship with the righteous man Noah. God commanded Noah to build an ark, saving his family and the animals from the flood. Afterwards, God made a covenant with Noah, promising never again to destroy the earth with a flood, and He set the rainbow as the sign of this covenant (Genesis 6-9).

column4: 4.  **Abraham (Abram)** - One of the most significant relationships in Genesis, God calls Abram to leave his homeland and promises to make him the father of a great nation. God establishes a covenant with Abram, promising land, descendants, and blessings for all nations through him. Abram’s faith and obedience become central themes, and his name is changed to Abraham as part of the covenant (Genesis 12, 15, 17, 22).
column5: 4.  **Abraham (Abram)** - As one of the most important relationships in Genesis, God calls Abram to leave his homeland and promises to make him the father of a great nation. Abram’s faith and obedience become central themes, and as part of the covenant his name is changed to Abraham (Genesis 12, 15, 17, 22).

column4: 5.  **Hagar** - An Egyptian servant of Sarah, Hagar encounters God in the wilderness after being mistreated. God comforts her, promises her a future for her son Ishmael, and instructs her to return to Abraham and Sarah. Hagar refers to God as “El Roi” (“The God Who Sees Me”), recognizing His care for her (Genesis 16).
column5: 5.  **Hagar** - Hagar, an Egyptian slave woman serving Sarah, after being mistreated, encounters God in the wilderness. column4: 6.  **Isaac** - The son of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac inherits the covenant promises made to his father. God reaffirms these promises directly to Isaac, including the promise of descendants and blessings. God also guides Isaac during a famine, protecting him and establishing the covenant relationship (Genesis 26).
column5: 6.  **Isaac** - Isaac, the son of Abraham and Sarah, inherits the covenant promises given to his father. column4: 7.  **Rebekah** - Although her relationship with God is indirect, God answers Rebekah’s prayer about her difficult pregnancy, revealing that her twins, Jacob and Esau, will become two nations with distinct destinies (Genesis 25).
column5: 7.  **Rebekah** - Though her relationship with God is indirect, God answers Rebekah’s prayer regarding her difficult pregnancy and reveals that her twins, Jacob and Esau, will become two nations with distinct destinies (Genesis 25).

column4: 8.  **Jacob** - God establishes a personal relationship with Jacob, appearing to him in a dream and confirming the covenant promises of land, descendants, and blessings. Jacob encounters God several times, including the famous wrestling match where God changes his name to Israel, symbolizing his transformation and the establishment of Israel as a people (Genesis 28, 32, 35).
column5: 8.  **Jacob** - God builds a personal relationship with Jacob, appears to him in dreams, and confirms the promises of the covenant concerning land, descendants, and blessing. column4: 9.  **Joseph** - Although Joseph’s relationship with God isn’t based on direct appearances or covenants like those of Abraham or Jacob, God is deeply involved in his life. Through dreams, divine favor, and providence, God guides Joseph’s journey from being sold into slavery to becoming a powerful leader in Egypt. Joseph’s faith in God’s sovereignty allows him to forgive his brothers, recognizing that God used his suffering for good (Genesis 37, 39-50).
column5: 9.  **Joseph** - Joseph’s relationship with God is not based on direct manifestations or a covenant like Abraham’s or Jacob’s, yet God is deeply involved in his life. Through dreams, divine favor, and providence, God guides Joseph from being sold as a slave to becoming a powerful leader in Egypt. Joseph’s faith in God’s sovereignty enabled him to acknowledge that God used his suffering for good and to forgive his brothers（Genesis 37, 39-50）.

column4: ### Exodus: The God Who Dwells With His People
column5: ### Exodus: God Who Dwells with His Own People

column4: God’s desire to dwell with His people is also clearly seen in the second book of the Bible, Exodus. In the book of the exodus the people of Israel, who had lived for a period of time in relative peace and harmony in Egypt, are now being oppressed by a Pharaoh who did not know of Joseph and feared the Hebrews (Exodus 1:6-8). God’s people lived in Egypt for roughly ~400 years (Exodus 12:40-41), of which the later portion of that was spent living as slaves (there is not a universal consensus on precisely how long Israel was in bondage to Egypt).
column5: God’s desire to dwell with His people is clearly seen in Exodus, the second book of the Bible. In Exodus, the people of Israel, who had once lived for a time in Egypt in relative peace and harmony, are now oppressed by a Pharaoh who did not know Joseph and feared the Hebrews（Exodus 1:6-8）. God’s people lived in Egypt for approximately ~400 years（Exodus 12:40-41）, and in the latter part of that period they lived as slaves (there is no universal agreement on the exact length of time Israel was under Egypt’s bondage).

column4: The phrase **“I AM THAT I AM”** (Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh) is one of the most profound self-revelations in Scripture. When Moses asks for God’s name, God responds with this phrase, which can be translated as "I Am Who I Am," "I Will Be Who I Will Be," or simply "I Am." This declaration on the surface is a bit confusing but holds deep meaning. Could you imagine introducing yourself to someone new as ‘I am’? When God reveals Himself as ‘I AM THAT I AM’ He is attesting to His nature, His eternal presence, His sovereignty. ‘I am’ is infinite in meaning and purpose.

column5: ### The Rest of the Old Testament

column4: In the ~1,400 years between the death of Moses and the birth of Christ the Israelites experienced a recurring cycle of devotion which brings God's favor and blessings, followed by rebellion, God’s judgment, their subsequent repentance, and ultimately God’s deliverance. This pattern is particularly evident in the books of **Judges, Kings, and Chronicles**, which recount cycles where the people turn away from God, often by worshiping other gods, resulting in periods of oppression or exile. In response to their cries, God repeatedly raised up judges, prophets, or leaders to deliver them.
column5: During the ~1,400 years from Moses’ death to the birth of Christ, Israel experienced a recurring cycle: receiving God’s grace and blessing through devotion, followed by rebellion, God’s judgment, repentance, and finally God’s salvation. This pattern is especially evident in **Judges, Kings, and Chronicles**, which record cycles in which the people turn away from God, often worshiping other gods, thereby bringing about periods of oppression and exile. In response to their cries, God repeatedly raised up judges, prophets, and leaders to deliver them.

column4: Throughout these years, despite the Israelites' frequent failures to uphold their covenant with Him, God remains faithful, showing both justice and mercy. He continuously rescues and forgives His people, demonstrating His enduring commitment and love.
column5: Throughout these years, despite Israel’s frequent failure to keep the covenant with God, He remained faithful and showed both justice and mercy. He continually rescued and forgave His people, revealing unwavering faithfulness and love.

column4: God’s character and actions are fully expressed in the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit. The scriptures teach that God is one in essence, yet exists as three distinct persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms God’s oneness, stating, “beside Him there is no God” (Isaiah 45:5). However, the Godhead is understood as a **compound unity**-three distinct persons who cooperate with a singular mind and purpose, united in the truest sense. Each person of the Trinity has a unique role: the **Father creates**, the **Son redeems**, and the **Holy Spirit sanctifies**. The term “Trinity” does not appear in the Bible; it was developed as a theological expression to describe this concept, which is revealed through Scripture.
column5: God’s nature and works are perfectly expressed in the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. Scripture teaches that God is one in essence, yet exists as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms God’s uniqueness, stating, "There is no God besides Me" (Isaiah 45:5). However, the Godhead is understood as a compound unity—three distinct persons who cooperate with a single mind and purpose. Each of the three has a unique role: **the Father creates**, **the Son redeems**, and **the Holy Spirit sanctifies**. The term "Trinity" does not appear in the Bible. It is a theological expression developed to describe this concept and is revealed throughout Scripture.

column4: The Trinity can be illustrated by examples in nature, which help clarify this idea of unity in diversity. Like water, which can be liquid, ice, or vapor but remains H₂O, each person of the Trinity is fully God yet distinct in personhood. Or consider a triangle, with three sides and three angles, forming one complete shape; if one side is removed, it ceases to be a triangle. Similarly, **God’s nature is incomplete without all three persons**, who work together in perfect unity.
column5: The Trinity can be illustrated by examples from nature, which help clarify the idea of unity in diversity. Just as water can be liquid, ice, or steam yet is essentially H₂O, each of the three is fully God while remaining distinct as persons. Or consider a triangle: its three sides and three angles form a single complete shape, but remove one side and it is no longer a triangle. Likewise, **without all three persons, God’s nature would not be complete**. The three work together in perfect unity.

column4: - **God the Father**: He is the creator and sustainer of all things, often understood as the initiator in the Godhead. His love for humanity is central to the biblical story, exemplified in John 3:16. In our study we will examine God the father as the loving father and righteous judge, who made a path for our redemption.
column5: - **God the Father**: the Creator and Sustainer of all things, often understood as the initiator within the Godhead. His love for humanity is central to the biblical narrative, exemplified by John 3:16. In this study, we consider God the Father as the loving Father and righteous Judge who has provided the way of our redemption.

column4: - **God the Son**: Co-existent and co-eternal with the Father, Jesus took on human nature, being conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life, died to redeem humanity, and rose again, defeating sin and death. He now sits at the Father’s right hand, interceding for us (John 1:1-3; Matthew 1:23; 1 Timothy 2:5). In our study we will examine Jesus as the perfect atoning sacrifice, the resurrected Lord, and head of the church.
column5: - **God the Son**: Jesus, coexistent and eternally equal with the Father, took on humanity, was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and was born of the virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life, died to redeem humanity, and rose again, triumphing over sin and death. He now sits at the right hand of the Father, interceding for us (John 1:1-3; Matthew 1:23; 1 Timothy 2:5). In this study, we consider Jesus as the perfect atoning sacrifice, the risen Lord, and the head of the Church.

column4: - **God the Holy Spirit**: The Holy Spirit, co-existent and equal with the Father and the Son, is sent by the Father through the Son to convict the world of sin and prepare believers as the Bride of Christ. He empowers, comforts, and sanctifies those who are in Christ (John 14:26; 15:26; 16:8). In our study we will examine the Holy Spirit as the comforter, given to us by God to equip, empower, sanctify, and abide with us.
column5: - **God the Holy Spirit**: The Holy Spirit, coexistent and equal with the Father and the Son, is sent by the Father through the Son to convict the world of sin and to prepare believers as the Bride of Christ. The Holy Spirit empowers, comforts, and sanctifies those who are in Christ (John 14:26; 15:26; 16:8). In this study, we consider the Holy Spirit as the Comforter who equips, empowers, sanctifies, and dwells with us.

column4: Through these distinct persons, God’s triune nature is revealed as a perfect union in purpose, will, and love, each person playing a vital role in the divine mission of creation, redemption, and sanctification. The Trinity invites believers to experience God fully, both as a loving Father, a redeeming Savior, and a transforming Spirit.

The Trinity invites believers to experience God in His fullness—as the loving Father, the redeeming Savior, and the transforming Spirit.

column4: ## Conclusion
column5: ## Conclusion

column4: We can be uniquely known by our names: husband, father, son, brother, friend. Each of these a declaration of who we are in relation to someone else. We can also be known by our attributes: faithful, patient, kind, intelligent, funny. Likewise, we can know God by His attributes and names- He is our Healer, Provider, Shepherd, and Redeemer. However, as labels and words are only a small part of us, for ourselves to be truly known by others, we must be experienced. Even more so with God. To truly and fully know Him we must experience Him.
column5: We can be uniquely known by names such as husband, father, son, brother, and friend. Each of these is a declaration of who we are in relation to someone. We are also known by attributes such as faithful, patient, kind, intelligent, and funny. Similarly, we can know God by His attributes and names - He is our healer, provider, shepherd, and redeemer. Yet labels and words are only a small part of us; to be truly known by others, we must be experienced. How much more so with God. To know God truly and fully, we must experience Him.

column4: God’s names reveal His character, but personal encounters deepen our understanding of what these names signify. For instance, “God my Healer” takes on a richer, more profound meaning when we understand the depths of illness, desperation, or helplessness from which God rescues. Knowing Him as our Provider is transformed when we have felt true need and found Him faithful.
column5: God’s names reveal His nature, but personal encounters deepen our understanding of what these names mean. For example, "God my Healer" takes on richer, deeper significance when we grasp the depths of the sickness, despair, or helplessness from which He delivers. Knowing God as Provider is likewise transformed when we feel real need and come to know that God is faithful.

column4: Scriptures offer a context to these encounters, showing us God’s faithfulness to His people across time and circumstance, reinforcing how His names and attributes are not mere titles but realities He brings to life, experienced in the lives of individuals. It is through this interplay of personal experience and the scriptural narrative that we come to know God-not just as a distant description but as a present, active relationship in every season of our lives.

We come to know God through this interplay of personal experience and the biblical narrative—not as a distant description, but as a present, active relationship in every season of our lives.
